sections.h2: Garland County and its school districts
sections.html:
Thermal springs, lakes and the Ouachita Mountains define Garland County, and Hot Springs serves as seat and biggest city. About 100,180 people lived here in 2020, spread over 735 square miles that include 57 of water. Lake Hamilton, Hot Springs Village, Rockwell, Piney, Mountain Pine, Fountain Lake and Lonsdale show up on the county map.

Five public school districts serve the city: Hot Springs, Lakeside, Cutter-Morning Star, Fountain Lake and Lake Hamilton. The district your house sits in sets part of the millage, so a house a few streets over can carry a different bill.

sections.h2: Property near the national park and lakes
sections.html:
Hot Springs National Park is the only national park in Arkansas, and the National Park Service manages it. Congress set aside the Hot Springs Reservation in 1832, the park was established in 1921, and a property dispute was settled in the federal government's favor by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1877. That history puts a federal boundary in the middle of the county seat.

If your house sits close to the park line or a lake shore, order a survey and ask the title company to look for easements or federal interests. A neighbor's description of the boundary is not a substitute for the recorded record.

Eight bathhouses stand along Central Avenue on Bathhouse Row, and that downtown stretch carries its own constraints. If your house is in an older part of town, ask the title company whether any recorded restriction or easement runs with the lot. Buyers' lenders tend to ask, and an answer ready in advance saves days.

The Assessor values property and the Tax Collector bills it. You will find both in the Government Office Building at 200 Woodbine Street, Hot Springs. The Assessor is at Suite 123, phone 501-622-3730.

The Tax Collector has been reported at Suite 108 with a 24-hour drop box behind the building, and the county's online payment page lists 501-622-3710. Call before you make a trip to confirm the office and its hours. The courthouse is at 501 Ouachita Avenue, phone 501-622-3600, and the county homepage has a tax and payment lookup on its quick links.

The real estate deadline is October 15, moving to the next business day when it lands on a weekend or holiday. Partial payments are generally accepted along the way. The county has charged a 3.8 percent card convenience fee that it does not keep, so ask what the current fee is before paying by card.

The owner of record on January 1 is the person assessed. After a sale, the recorded deed is what puts the buyer's name on the roll, which is why timely recording matters.

Deadline or stepDateWhat it means
Pay real estate taxOctober 15, or the next business dayPartial payments generally accepted until then

Delinquent listBy December 1Sent for newspaper publication

Penalty and fee amounts can change, so confirm them with the collector.

The state requires reappraisal on a 3, 4 or 5 year schedule. Garland County reported a five-year cycle in 2019 and hired an outside appraisal firm. Assessed value runs at 20 percent of market value.

Under Amendment 79, assessed value is frozen for owner-occupied homes of seniors and disabled owners, and yearly increases on owner-occupied homes cannot exceed 5 percent. So a house that gained more than 25 percent over a five-year cycle is not taxed at its full new value the moment the next cycle ends.

Think the value is off? Phone the Assessor, because wrong square footage or room counts can be fixed informally. A real disagreement over value goes to the County Board of Equalization, and you must schedule by the third Monday in August.

Millage varies from one town to the next. In late 2019 the Quorum Court ratified rates that included a rollback for Mountain Pine's general fund, from 5 mills to 4.9 mills. State law requires a rollback when a tax base grows by more than 10 percent, and Mountain Pine's taxable assessed value had risen 11.51 percent, helped by close to $1 million in new construction, mostly a plant finished in 2018 and assessed in 2019.

A new plant, subdivision or lake development can move a bill. If you are comparing parcels, ask for the current millage for the specific school district and city.

Request a statement for the parcel from the Collector and let the title company settle the balance out of proceeds. The Garland County Circuit Clerk records the deed. A state transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration applies to deals above $100.

Taxes left unpaid can lead to an auction of delinquent land by the Commissioner of State Lands. Act 241, effective July 1, 2023, made auction sales final. The redemption right ends at 4 p.m. on the last business day before the sale, so clear any delinquency well ahead of that.

  • Order a survey when the lot is near a lake or the park boundary.
  • Check the school district and any improvement district on the bill.
  • Collect permits for lakefront or older downtown work.
  • Ask the Tax Collector whether a prior-year balance or penalty is attached to the parcel.
  • Photograph any repairs you finished so a buyer can see the condition.

After you shake hands on a price, a title company opens a file and searches the parcel record. It turns up the tax balance, liens and recorded easements. Expect a few questions about who holds title, whether a lake or park boundary touches the lot and whether an improvement district charge sits on the bill.

Closing day is mostly signing. The deed goes to the Circuit Clerk, the Collector gets paid from proceeds, and the next bill belongs to the buyer once the deed is on record.

An heir selling from another state can do nearly all of this by phone and mail. Request the balance in writing and keep the receipt.

A regular listing in Hot Springs brings repairs, showings, an inspection and a lender's appraisal. Rain adds to it: the area gets about 58 inches a year and May is the wettest month, so roofs, crawl spaces and grading on older downtown and lakefront houses draw a close look.

A cash buyer who takes the house as is drops the repair list. Tax payoff, recording and disclosure still happen. What changes is the calendar: closing follows your date, which suits heirs, relocating owners and anyone carrying two houses.

Have your last tax statement, deed, any survey and permit records ready. Lay the written offer beside the tax payoff to see your net.

faqs.q: Where is the Garland County Assessor?
faqs.a: Go to 200 Woodbine, Suite 123, Hot Springs, AR 71901, or call 501-622-3730.

faqs.q: When is the Garland County property tax deadline?
faqs.a: October 15. A weekend or holiday moves it to the next business day, and partial payments are generally accepted.

faqs.q: How do I appeal a Garland County assessment?
faqs.a: Talk to the Assessor, then ask for a Board of Equalization hearing before the third Monday in August.

faqs.q: Is land inside Hot Springs National Park taxable?
faqs.a: The park is federal land, established in 1921. A parcel near the line deserves a title company check.

faqs.q: Can a Garland County house with unpaid taxes still be sold?
faqs.a: Yes, provided the balance is paid at closing before any auction. Once the Commissioner of State Lands sells at auction, Act 241 makes it final.
